place: Red Cloud Agency, Nebraska; Spotted Tail Agency, Nebraska
instrument: Agreement with the Sioux (and Northern Cheyenne/Arapaho), Sept 26, 1876 (Black Hills / Manypenny agreement)
summary: The report reprints the 1876 agreement text, including Article 6 promising a house for each principal chief if the Indians removed to Indian Territory. The author's endnote calls this an unlawful use of bribery in Indian politics.
verbatim_quote: the Government shall erect for each of the principal chiefs a good and comfortable dwelling-house.
federal_account_contrast: Kappler/federal record presents the agreement as a consensual cession; source frames the chief-house clause as a bribe tied to removal.
map_implication: Tag the 1876/1877 agreement (Black Hills cession) with a 'bribery inducement alleged' note for Cheyenne signers.
notes: Ratified by Act of Feb 28, 1877 (19 Stat. 254) per general knowledge, not cited in this chunk. Royce area for 1877 Black Hills cession not given by source; verify (likely Royce 1, 2 area for Sioux, Royce schedule 1877).

place: Red Cloud Agency and Spotted Tail Agency, Nebraska
instrument: Agreement of Sept 26, 1876; Cheyenne signatures dated Spotted Tail Agency Sept 28, 1877
summary: The signature block shows Cheyenne marks (Living Bear, Spotted Elk, Black Bear, Turkey Legs, Calfskin Shirt) appended at Spotted Tail Agency on Sept 28, 1877, a year after the commissioners signed. Elsewhere the author states no Northern Cheyenne leader legally signed the 1877 agreement.
verbatim_quote: Dated and signed at Spotted Tail Agency, Nebraska, September 28, 1877.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty signature block reprinted; p. 321 narrative
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats the agreement as binding on the Northern Cheyenne; the source says Cheyenne signers were few and lacked authority, and signed after Congress had already enacted it.
map_implication: Show the Northern Cheyenne as non-consenting party to the 1876-77 agreement; note signature date discrepancy.
notes: Text extraction puts Little Wolf under 'Arapahos'; layout may be garbled. Calfskin Shirt is the father of Bear Bow (see p. 328 finding).

nations: Northern Cheyenne; Northern Arapaho; Southern Cheyenne; Southern Arapaho
place: Medicine Lodge reservation (Indian Territory); Great Sioux Reservation
instrument: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, May 10, 1868 (Fort Laramie)
summary: Author argues that because the U.S. never located the Northern Cheyenne on either of the two reservations the 1868 treaty named (Medicine Lodge lands, which were disputed and too small, or the Sioux reservation), their forfeiture of 'territory outside of the two reservations' is void and they retain a legitimate land claim.
verbatim_quote: The failure to fulfill locating the Northern Cheyenne within the agreed upon locations vacates the forfeiture of their "territory outside of the two reservations mentioned above."
federal_account_contrast: Royce treats the 1868 relinquishment as an effective cession; source asserts it is void for U.S. non-performance.
map_implication: Flag the 1868 Northern Cheyenne-Arapaho relinquishment as 'conditional cession, condition unfulfilled' in Indigenous view.
notes: Legal argument by the author, not a court holding.

instrument: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, May 10, 1868
summary: Author says the U.S. lacked authority to assign the Northern Cheyenne land inside the existing Sioux reservation, since the 1868 Sioux treaty reserved no such right.
verbatim_quote: the U.S. government did not have the authority to assign land within the boundaries of an existing reservation.
federal_account_contrast: Federal framing treats the option to join the Sioux as a valid treaty term.
map_implication: Note that the 1868 'attach to Sioux reservation' option conflicted with Sioux treaty rights.

instrument: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, 1868, Article 2
summary: Author says ambiguous Article 2 language left the Northern Cheyenne without a permanent reservation until 1884, effectively exiled in their homeland for twenty years.
verbatim_quote: Essentially the Northern Cheyenne were exiled in their homeland for twenty years.
federal_account_contrast: Adds the human cost of the 16-year gap between 1868 and the 1884 executive order.
map_implication: Timeline: mark 1868-1884 as a period with no secure Northern Cheyenne land base.

instrument: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, 1868
summary: Author states the 1868 treaty was made by a limited number of people, none with authority to bind the whole people, and that handwritten council transcripts show the farming provisions were rejected.
verbatim_quote: Many people today have concluded that the Treaty of 1868 was made by a limited number of People, and none of those had the authority to bind all the People to this treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 34, 35 (references handwritten transcripts, not cited specifically)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record lists the signers as representative chiefs.
map_implication: Flag 1868 Northern Cheyenne-Arapaho treaty: signer authority contested.
notes: Transcripts referenced but not cited; verify against the 1868 council proceedings.

instrument: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, 1868 (article on Army officer attesting delivery of goods)
instrument_cite: H.R. Rep. No. 98, 42nd Cong., 3rd Sess. (1872), Investigation of Indian Frauds
summary: The treaty clause requiring an Army officer to attest annuity deliveries is called a failure because of widespread fraud in Indian Country, citing the 1872 House frauds investigation.
verbatim_quote: This was an absolute miserable failure because of the fraud that happened during this time in Indian Country.
federal_account_contrast: Adds that annuity terms the map may treat as compensation were not delivered as promised.
map_implication: Attach annuity-fraud note to 1868 treaty record; cite H.R. Rep. 98, 42-3.

instrument: 1876-77 Agreement relinquishing hunting rights; Fort Laramie Treaty 1868
summary: Author states that hunting rights could not be abrogated, nor territory relinquished, without approval of a majority of adults under the 1868 treaty, so the 1877 agreement's relinquishment was invalid.
verbatim_quote: the hunting rights could not be abrogated without the majority of the adults approving the action.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 54 (cites Article 8, Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868)
federal_account_contrast: Parallel to the Sioux three-fourths clause argument; federal record treats 1877 as effective.
map_implication: Mark the 1877 relinquishment of Cheyenne hunting rights/territory as lacking required adult consent.
notes: Source cites 'Article 8'; the well-known 3/4 adult male consent clause is Article 12 of the 1868 Sioux treaty. Verify which article and treaty the author means.

summary: Author notes several 1877 agreement provisions (allotment selection, on-reservation obligations) could never be performed by the Cheyenne because most had already been moved to Oklahoma, which commissioners must have known.
verbatim_quote: This would have been nearly impossible for the Cheyenne since the majority of them had already been moved to Oklahoma.
federal_account_contrast: Shows agreement terms were drafted around a removal already under way.
map_implication: Link 1877 agreement to Northern Cheyenne removal to Indian Territory.
notes: Chronology: removal south was summer 1877; Cheyenne signatures Sept 1877. Worth checking.

place: Powder River Country, Montana, to Indian Territory (Darlington / Fort Reno agency area; source says Fort Sill)
summary: After surrendering in 1877, the Northern Cheyenne were force-relocated by the Army to Indian Territory, where as many as one-third died of disease (dysentery, influenza, malaria). Grinnell: nearly two-thirds of 999 were sick within two months; 41 died the first winter, and Cheyenne sources put deaths much higher.
verbatim_quote: as many as one-third of the interned Cheyenne died of disease
sources_cited_by_source: Sandoz 1964, 27-28; Grinnell 1956, 400; Little Chief testimony to Congressional committee 1878 (Grinnell 401)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record frames 1877 as consolidation with Southern kin under treaty; source frames it as forced internment with mass death.
map_implication: Draw removal route Powder River to Indian Territory 1877; add mortality note.
notes: Source repeatedly says 'Fort Sill'; the Northern Cheyenne were held at the Cheyenne-Arapaho (Darlington) agency near Fort Reno. Likely a source error. Mortality figures differ (one-third vs 41 deaths).

summary: Source summarizes that warfare marked by the slaughter of perhaps half the Cheyenne at Sand Creek, the Washita, and Sappa Creek preceded the 1877 surrender.
verbatim_quote: in warfare marked by the slaughter of perhaps half their number at places such as Sand Creek, the Washita, and Sappa Creek
federal_account_contrast: Sappa Creek (1875) is rarely in federal treaty-based records.
map_implication: Ensure Sappa Creek (Kansas, April 1875) is included in massacre layer alongside Sand Creek and Washita.
notes: 'Half their number' is a broad estimate.

summary: On Sept 9, 1878, about 350 Northern Cheyenne (92 fighting-age men, 261 women, children, elderly) under Dull Knife and Little Wolf left Indian Territory for the north, eluding up to 13,000 troops over 1,000 miles.
verbatim_quote: it was far better to die trying to return home than to stay and resign themselves to a tragic death from disease or starvation.
sources_cited_by_source: Gerry Robinson (Northern Cheyenne), WYOHistory.org; Sandoz 1964, 147; Andrist 1964, 321
federal_account_contrast: Federal record calls this an outbreak; source frames it as a flight home from deadly internment.
map_implication: Draw 1878 Northern Cheyenne exodus route as a story line.

summary: Dull Knife's band of 149 (46 men, 61 women, 42 children) was captured Oct 23, 1878, disarmed, horses impounded, and interned in a barracks at Camp Robinson. Officials secretly arranged a second forced relocation south and the Kansas governor's demand for trial of leaders.
verbatim_quote: We are back on our own ground, and have stopped fighting. We have found the place we started to come to.
sources_cited_by_source: Powell 1969, 217-225; Grinnell 1956, 417; Military Division of the Missouri Briefs 9079, 9421, 9983, 10209, 10315
federal_account_contrast: Adds archival military correspondence showing the return south was decided without the prisoners' knowledge.
map_implication: Mark Fort Robinson as internment site of Dull Knife's band 1878-79.

summary: After the Cheyenne refused to return south, Capt. Henry W. Wessells cut off food and firewood on Jan 4 and water on Jan 8, 1879, in subzero weather, and put Wild Hog in irons on Jan 9, to force consent to removal.
verbatim_quote: Wessells immediately began attempting to "change their minds" by cutting off their food and firewood, escalating on January 8 to cutting off their water.
sources_cited_by_source: War Dept. 1879 Board of Officers 'Proceedings', RG 98 NARA, Wessells testimony 75-79; Powell 1969, 231-232; Grinnell 1956, 425-426
federal_account_contrast: A textbook case of starvation used to compel a removal; the Army's own court of inquiry documents it.
map_implication: Tag Fort Robinson 1879 with DURESS_STARVATION (food, fuel, water withheld) and HOSTAGE (leaders in irons).
notes: Some Cheyenne say water and fuel were cut off for the full eight days (endnote 31).

place: Camp Robinson, White River, and Pine Ridge escarpment, Nebraska; final washout ~35 mi NNW of Camp Robinson on Warbonnet/Antelope Creek
summary: On the night of Jan 9, 1879, about 130 starving prisoners broke out; troops rode people down in the snow and civilians executed wounded and mutilated women. Pursuit ended Jan 22 when troops fired volleys into a washout, killing all the men. Army count: 64 Cheyenne dead, 78 captured, 7 unaccounted.
verbatim_quote: the troops simply rode people down, shooting them and leaving them to freeze where they fell
sources_cited_by_source: War Dept. 1879 'Proceedings' (testimony of Cummings, Baxter, Pettys, Simpson); Powell 1969; Sandoz 1964; Grinnell 1956; Bronson 1908; Ricker Tablets
federal_account_contrast: Federal sources call it the 'Fort Robinson outbreak'; the report calls it the Fort Robinson Massacre (p. 337).
map_implication: Add Fort Robinson Massacre (Jan 9-22, 1879) to massacre layer with points at Fort Robinson and the final washout.
notes: Casualty counts vary: Wessells 'about 30' first night vs burial detail 'about fifty' (Grinnell 423); Cummings 39 men and 22 women and children.

place: White River near Camp Robinson, Nebraska
summary: Army officers testified that civilians (trader J.W. Dear, Henry Clifford) followed troops killing wounded Cheyenne and mutilating bodies, including sexual violation of dead women. Wounded children included infants who died of gunshot wounds.
verbatim_quote: As there were no soldiers there, I was convinced that these civilians were killing wounded Indians.
sources_cited_by_source: 'Proceedings' 1879, Cummings testimony 167-169; List of Indians Wounded 139-140; Ricker Tablets vol. 2, 289
federal_account_contrast: Civilian atrocities absent from treaty-based records.
map_implication: Include civilian participation and child casualties in the Fort Robinson massacre record.
notes: Clifford denied the charges (Proceedings 161-165).

place: Fort Leavenworth / Kansas; back to Indian Territory
summary: Seven surviving men (Wild Hog, Tangle Hair, Left Hand, Old Crow, Porcupine, Blacksmith, Noisy Walker) were shipped to Kansas for trial demanded by the Kansas governor, acquitted for lack of evidence, then sent back to Indian Territory. Wild Hog and his wife tried to stab themselves rather than go south.
verbatim_quote: All were ultimately acquitted of any criminal actions, but they were then returned to Fort Sill, Oklahoma.
sources_cited_by_source: 18th Biennial Report, Kansas State Historical Society 1910-12; Powell 1969, 273-274; Sandoz 1964, 270
federal_account_contrast: State prosecution as an arm of removal.
map_implication: Note Kansas state role in prosecuting Northern Cheyenne exodus leaders.

place: Pine Ridge; Fort Keogh (Miles City, MT); Tongue River
summary: Survivors (about 58 women, children and elders) were sent to Pine Ridge on Jan 31, 1879; Dull Knife reached Pine Ridge separately; Little Wolf's band of 112 surrendered March 25, 1879 to Lt. W.P. Clark and was allowed to stay. The report says the breakouts forced creation of a Montana reservation.
verbatim_quote: The breakouts of 1878-79 had achieved one accomplishment: they had forced the U.S. Congress to establish a reservation in Montana.
federal_account_contrast: The source credits Cheyenne resistance, not federal grant, for the reservation.
map_implication: Link Northern Cheyenne Reservation origin to the 1878-79 exodus.
notes: The reservation was created by executive order (1884), not Congress; the source wording is loose.

instrument: Executive Order of Nov 26, 1884 creating Tongue River (Northern Cheyenne) Reservation
summary: The reservation (371,200 acres, 680 sq mi) was made by executive order, which the author calls legally questionable because the 1865, 1868 treaties and 1877 agreement confirmed a northern reservation on land the Cheyenne legally possessed. Boundaries excluded Cheyenne families homesteading near the Tongue River.
verbatim_quote: Did the Cheyenne honestly give up their rights to land in the north?
federal_account_contrast: Atlas likely shows EO reservation as a grant; source says it shrank land the Cheyenne never ceded.
map_implication: Draw the 1884 EO boundary (371,200 acres) and mark surrounding Powder River/Tongue River lands as never-validly-ceded per source.
notes: p. 322 quote gives 'Executive Order on 16 November 1884' vs 26 November elsewhere; the commonly cited date is Nov 26, 1884.

place: West bank / east of Tongue River, Montana
instrument: Executive Order of March 19, 1900 (McKinley) extending reservation
summary: The 1900 extension to the Tongue River raised the reservation to 444,157 acres, but Cheyenne who had homesteaded east of the river were relocated west of it; whites had already homesteaded most of the area.
verbatim_quote: Those who had homesteaded east of the Tongue River were relocated to the west of the river.
federal_account_contrast: Adds a small internal removal hidden inside a boundary 'expansion'.
map_implication: Draw 1900 extension boundary to Tongue River; note Cheyenne homesteaders east of river displaced.

place: Northern Cheyenne Reservation; St. Labre Mission, Ashland, MT
instrument: Courts of Indian Offenses (Commissioner Hiram Price, 1883); Cheyenne Court of Indian Offenses 1889; Sun Dance ban 1880
summary: The BIA and Catholic and Mennonite missions suppressed Cheyenne religion: Courts of Indian Offenses (1883; Cheyenne court 1889) punished dances and medicine men, the Sun Dance was banned around 1880 for about 50 years, and the Council of 44 lost authority to the agent.
verbatim_quote: The suppression of the Sun Dance continued for approximately 50 years.
sources_cited_by_source: Prucha 1984; Pahr 1997; Stands in Timber & Liberty 1967; Weist 1977; Moore 1974
federal_account_contrast: Cultural suppression not part of land records but tied to reservation confinement.
map_implication: Optional: add reservation-era religious suppression context to the Northern Cheyenne reservation entry.

place: Near present Chief Dull Knife College, Lame Deer, Northern Cheyenne Reservation, MT
summary: Head Chief and 13-year-old Young Mule were killed by about 90 First Cavalry troops after Head Chief killed a white man who was illegally on the reservation grazing cattle; the agent rejected the tribal offer of 30 horses as compensation.
verbatim_quote: The man was illegally on the reservation, and his cows were grazing illegally on Cheyenne land.
federal_account_contrast: Shows ongoing trespass on the reservation and military enforcement.
map_implication: Optional point: Head Chief and Young Mule, 1890.

place: White River, Pine Ridge Reservation, SD; Busby, MT
summary: The White River Cheyenne, living at Pine Ridge since 1879, were allowed to join the Northern Cheyenne Reservation in 1890-91 over BIA opposition; some stayed with Oglala kin.
verbatim_quote: General Miles had suggested this recommendation, but the Bureau of Indian Affairs opposed it.
federal_account_contrast: Oral source for a relocation not in treaty records.
map_implication: Note White River Cheyenne relocation Pine Ridge to Busby 1890-91.
notes: Text says 1890 in narrative and 1891 in band addendum.

place: Red Cloud Agency area; Black Hills; El Reno, OK (affidavit)
summary: In a sworn 1918 statement, Bear Bow, son of signer Calf Skin Shirt, said his father understood the 1876 agreement as allowing whites to mine Black Hills gold for half the gold, not a sale, and that only about one-sixth of the Cheyenne (friendly bands and Army scouts) were present and had no authority to sign for the rest.
verbatim_quote: they made a treaty with the commissioners giving the white people the right to mine gold in the Black Hills for half of the gold mined, but they did not sell the Black Hills.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows a cession of the Black Hills; Cheyenne account says it was a mining-share arrangement by an unauthorized minority.
map_implication: Flag the 1877 Black Hills cession as contested by Cheyenne testimony (gold-sharing, not sale; 1/6 present).
notes: Single affidavit, 42 years after the event; interpreted by Robert Burns.

nations: Northern Cheyenne; Southern Cheyenne; Arapaho; Lakota
place: Black Hills and lands south of the North Platte
summary: Cheyenne joined to claim the Black Hills; the 1851 treaty assigned Cheyenne-Arapaho lands south of the North Platte but Article 5 preserved claims to other lands and hunting rights. A Black Hills claim was filed in 1926.
verbatim_quote: the aforesaid Indian nations do not hereby abandon or prejudice any rights or claims they may have to other lands
federal_account_contrast: Atlas may show Black Hills as solely Lakota; source asserts a Cheyenne claim too.
map_implication: Indicate Cheyenne claim to Black Hills as overlapping; note 1926 claim filing.
notes: 1926 claim not otherwise identified; verify (possibly Court of Claims petition).

summary: From about 1919 the BIA killed up to 100 Cheyenne horses a month, paying $6.50 per hide, to make room for cattle; the herd fell from 15,000 to 3,000 by 1930, and the BIA-run tribal cattle herd failed within five years.
verbatim_quote: As many as 100 horses were killed monthly, and the owner received a measly $6.50 per hide.
map_implication: Context only.

instrument: Allotment of Northern Cheyenne Reservation (completed 1932); IRA Constitution 1936
summary: Under heavy BIA pressure the Cheyenne voted to allot; 1,457 members got 160 acres, there was not enough land, and allotment let many non-Indians buy and lease reservation land. The 1936 IRA constitution vote is called suspicious.
verbatim_quote: Under tremendous pressure from the Bureau of Indian Affairs, Cheyenne tribal members voted to allot their reservation lands.
federal_account_contrast: Allotment framed as tribal choice in federal record; source stresses coercion.
map_implication: Note allotment-era land loss within the Northern Cheyenne Reservation.
notes: Category DURESS_MILITARY used loosely for administrative pressure; consider OTHER. Allotment act cite not given (likely Act of June 3, 1926).

nations: Northern Cheyenne; Northern Arapaho; Southern Cheyenne; Southern Arapaho
place: Fort Laramie (Horse Creek) 1851 Cheyenne-Arapaho territory: Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming
summary: The ICC took the 51,210,000-acre 1851 territory as the claim area, valued it at $23,500,000 as of Oct 14, 1865, averaging 46 cents an acre, then accepted a $15 million compromise for the Oklahoma claims offered by attorney William Payne. Final recommendation Oct 18, 1965.
verbatim_quote: The Commission determined that the 1851 Horse Creek Treaty lands, which comprise 51,210,000 acres, would serve as the basis for the claim and determined its value to be $23,500,000.
sources_cited_by_source: ICC reports as cited; Perkinson 1993 (Deloria class)
federal_account_contrast: Federal/ICC record treats the payment as full extinguishment; source calls the valuation arbitrary and the compromise negligent.
map_implication: On 1851 Cheyenne-Arapaho polygon, note ICC extinguishment by payment (Dockets 329/348), 46 cents/acre, 1865 dollars, no land returned.
notes: Source calls Payne's offer 'negligent': an author judgment.

instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas, Oct 14, 1865 (used as ICC taking date)
summary: Both sides' attorneys stipulated the 1865 Little Arkansas treaty date as the taking date, which lowered value: mining was in a slump and railroads had not yet crossed the land. The author notes the 1865 treaty did not apply to the Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho at all.
verbatim_quote: First, the 1865 Treaty did not apply to Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho; second, the 1865 Treaty should never have been ratified
federal_account_contrast: The ICC used a treaty the Northern Cheyenne never signed as the date their land was 'taken'.
map_implication: Note that the ICC valuation date (Oct 14, 1865) rests on a treaty not involving the Northern Cheyenne.

summary: The ICC allowed offsets from four treaties, so the government 'bought' the tract four times for offset purposes. Consideration for Southern Cheyenne-Arapaho was $1,434,131.38; the government sought $7 million more in gratuitous offsets; boarding schools were counted as offsets.
verbatim_quote: although the land changed hands only once for legal purposes, the government bought the tract four separate times for offset purposes.
federal_account_contrast: Offsets included unwanted expenditures such as boarding schools.
map_implication: Record offset structure in ICC data for the 1851 Cheyenne-Arapaho claim.

summary: The ICC paid no interest, settling in 1865 dollars; at 5% compounded over 100 years the payment would have been about 130 times larger, over $1.5 billion.
verbatim_quote: the Cheyenne payment would have increased by 130 times the original amount, exceeding $1.5 billion!
sources_cited_by_source: Carlson 1985, in Sutton ed., Irredeemable America, 97-99
federal_account_contrast: Shows 'compensation' was a fraction of value.
map_implication: Display ICC award alongside interest-adjusted value.

instrument: ICC compromise settlement, Northern Cheyenne Indians of the Tongue River Reservation, Docket 329-C (with 348)
summary: Northern Cheyenne interlocutory award was $5,360,886.19 before offsets; the U.S. claimed $3,213,580.46 offsets; the compromise deducted $1,000,000 for a net $4,360,886.19 which also released accounting, rights-of-way, buffalo/timber/grass destruction, and intentional tort claims including wrongful attacks and wrongful removal.
verbatim_quote: a net judgment for the petitioner of $4,360,886.19 was considered somewhat more than the probable value of the Fort Laramie land cession claim alone
sources_cited_by_source: ICC settlement transcript (counsel Charles A. Hobbs, Wilkinson, Cragun & Barker); 13 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1
federal_account_contrast: Massacre and removal claims were extinguished as part of a land settlement, never heard.
map_implication: Note that Northern Cheyenne tort claims (wrongful attacks, wrongful removal) were released in the 1963 ICC compromise.

instrument: Congressional appropriation and distribution of ICC award
summary: After legal fees the Northern Cheyenne got under $4 million for more than 12,500,000 acres, distributed per capita; the BIA released only $100 of each $1,000 share and required business plans for the rest.
verbatim_quote: the Northern Cheyenne received a credit of less than $4 million for more than 12,500,000 acres of land!
sources_cited_by_source: 16 ICC 162, 178; interview with Dennis Limberhand, May 2023; Perkinson 1993
map_implication: Show Northern Cheyenne share as roughly 12.5 million acres for under $4 million (about 32 cents/acre before fees).
notes: Mix of ICC citation and oral interview.

summary: The author argues the Northern Cheyenne had inadequate representation: tribal attorneys (BIA-approved) talked clients out of claims filed by Rufus Wallowing in Docket 348 and merged them, saying they had little merit.
verbatim_quote: the attorney representing the Tribes inserted a false claim that the claims requested by Rufus Wallowing had little or no merit.
sources_cited_by_source: ICC Vol. 13 No. 1; ICC Act Sec. 2
map_implication: Note conflict-of-interest critique of the ICC Northern Cheyenne settlement.

instrument_cite: Kappler vol. II, 594-596; Royce, Indian Land Cessions, 786-787 n.1; Prucha 1994, 440-447
summary: The author asserts the 1851 treaty was never ratified (recorded as ratified, later corrected to not ratified), so the ICC should not have used it to compute a settlement.
verbatim_quote: However, the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1851 was never ratified.
federal_account_contrast: Contested: the Senate amended the annuity term (50 to 10 years) and the treaty is generally treated as in force via appropriations; its formal status is debated.
map_implication: Mark 1851 Fort Laramie as 'ratification status contested; Senate amendment' rather than plain ratified.

summary: The ICC record acknowledged the buffalo's central role but gave no compensation for loss of the buffalo economy, which the author calls an additional treaty violation of 1851 Art. 5 and 1868 Art. 2 hunting rights.
verbatim_quote: Despite being mentioned, there was no consideration for compensation for the economic loss of Buffalo.
sources_cited_by_source: Fort Laramie 1851 Art. 5; 1868 Northern Cheyenne-Arapaho treaty Art. 2 (Kappler 1012)
map_implication: Note uncompensated hunting rights/buffalo loss on the 1851 polygon.

place: Colorado Front Range; Pike's Peak gold region; Denver
instrument: Indian Trade and Intercourse Act of 1834, Sec. 11
summary: Up to 100,000 gold-rush trespassers occupied Cheyenne-Arapaho land in Colorado (1858-61) in violation of the 1834 Act, which required $1,000 fines and removal; $15,307,000 in minerals was taken 1859-1865 before any cession. Sen. Stephen Douglas said in 1858 that every man at Pike's Peak was there illegally.
verbatim_quote: Every man in Pike's Peak is there in violation of the law
sources_cited_by_source: Douglas, Senate 1858 (no page cite); Intercourse Act 1834 Sec. 11 quoted
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows these lands as ceded by later treaty; the source stresses years of illegal occupation and extraction before any cession.
map_implication: Shade Colorado Front Range as 'occupied illegally 1858-1861 before any cession'; note $15.3M mineral extraction.
notes: Mineral figure lacks a specific citation in text.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb 18, 1861 (Article 11 struck by Senate); Congressional Act of 1864 transferring land to Denver
summary: The Senate struck Article 11 (which had Denver-area lands priced at $1.25 an acre) without returning the amended treaty to the tribes; an Aug 12, 1861 State Department letter asked that tribal assent be obtained, with no evidence it was. Cheyenne chiefs denied signing, and an 1864 Act of Congress transferred land to Denver without tribal permission.
verbatim_quote: as it does not from the face of the paper that the amendment referred to has been agreed to by the Indian Tribes concerned, through their proper representatives
sources_cited_by_source: Seward to Dole, Aug 12, 1861, Domestic Letters vol. 54, 440; BIA Reports 1865, 248; Colley to CIA, Sept 30, 1863, Upper Arkansas Agency, RG 75
federal_account_contrast: Federal record lists Fort Wise as ratified; source shows the State Department itself flagged missing tribal consent to the amendment.
map_implication: Flag Fort Wise 1861 as SENATE_AMENDED_NO_CONSENT; flag Denver townsite land as transferred without title.
notes: 1864 Denver act not cited by Stat. page in the source; verify.

summary: Territorial Governor and Superintendent John Evans chose to 'eliminate Indians' rather than remove trespassers as the 1834 Act and 1851 treaty required, and profited personally.
verbatim_quote: John Evans, decided to "Eliminate Indians" and not remove trespassers as legally required
map_implication: Attach Evans' dual role as governor/superintendent to Colorado land takings.

place: Cheyenne lands north of South Platte
summary: Author lists remaining legal options: land return (citing Taos Blue Lake 1970), buffalo-slaughter hunting-rights claims north of the South Platte, accounting claims for stock-raising and minerals, trespass income, and war-crimes claims for Sand Creek and the Fort Robinson Massacre. He notes the Flute case was not allowed to be heard.
verbatim_quote: The Sand Creek and Fort Robinson Massacres were unprovoked attacks on civilian targets and could form the basis for other suits.
map_implication: Possible note on unresolved claims.
notes: The 'Flute case' is not otherwise identified; verify.

instrument: BIA-approved coal leases and permits 1966, 1969, 1971; Interior Sec. Morton ruling June 4, 1974; Act of Congress 1980 cancelling leases
summary: Between 1966 and 1971 the BIA approved coal leases and permits covering 214,000 acres, half the reservation, with inadequate royalties and no proper environmental review. The tribe sought cancellation; Morton's 1974 ruling required tribal agreement before mining, and Congress cancelled the leases in 1980.
verbatim_quote: the BIA approved coal mining leases and exploratory permits with outside corporations that covered 214.000 Northern Cheyenne acres, one-half the reservation.
sources_cited_by_source: Harris & Harris 1977, Indians, Coal, and the Big Sky; Dennis Limberhand interview
federal_account_contrast: Trust breach by the BIA.
map_implication: Optional: note 1966-71 BIA coal leases on half the reservation and their cancellation.
notes: 1980 act likely Pub. L. 96-401 (Northern Cheyenne Lands Act amendments); not cited in source, verify.

summary: Colorado compensate the Northern Cheyenne for pain and suffering from illegal trespass under the 1834 Intercourse Act.
verbatim_quote: It is recommended that the State of Colorado compensate the Northern Cheyenne Tribe for pain and suffering (and/or mental distress) resulting from illegal trespass.
federal_account_contrast: Restorative-justice proposals with no federal-record counterpart.
map_implication: Include in recommendations layer / Colorado context panel.
